description: Master source utility, compare interpretations and tackle the 12-mark and 16-mark essays.
content_html:
What the Exam Tests: The Key Question Types

Exam questions on this unit test a set of specific historical skills. Understanding exactly what each question type is asking — and what the most common mistakes are — is as important as knowing the content. This lesson works through the main question types, using worked examples from the period 1890–1918.

Key Fact

For Source Utility questions (5 marks), the three elements that must work together are: Content (what the source actually says), Provenance (who produced it, when, why, for what audience) and Contextual knowledge (what you know from your own learning that helps you assess the source).

Source Utility: The 5-Mark Question

The most common mistake on source utility questions is judging a source purely on bias: “This source is biased because it was written by a government minister, so it is not useful.” This always misses the point. A source’s utility must be assessed for a specific enquiry. A government propaganda poster is extremely useful as evidence of what the government wanted people to believe — its “bias” is precisely what makes it valuable for that enquiry.

A strong utility answer does three things in sequence. First, it identifies what the source says (content). Second, it comments on who produced it and why (provenance). Third, it uses own knowledge to explain what this tells us about the source’s value for the specific question asked. All three elements should be present in a single integrated judgement, not three separate bullet points.

Question: How useful is a Charles Booth survey extract (describing families in East London living on less than 21 shillings per week) for understanding the case for Liberal social reform?

Weak answer: “This source is useful because Booth was a reliable researcher. He found lots of poverty.” (No provenance, no contextual knowledge, no specific claim about utility.)

Strong answer structure: “This source is useful for understanding the case for reform because it shows [content: specific detail from extract]. Booth was a wealthy Liverpool businessman who surveyed London from the 1880s to 1903 with no financial interest in exaggerating poverty — this increases the reliability of the content [provenance]. My own knowledge confirms that Booth found roughly 30 per cent of Londoners in poverty and identified structural causes rather than personal failings, which directly influenced Liberal reform arguments after 1906 [contextual knowledge]. However, the source is limited for understanding what form the reforms should take, since Booth described the problem rather than prescribing solutions.”

The Compare Interpretations Question (10 marks)

The critical rule for this question: you must explain why the interpretations differ, not just how they differ. Describing “Interpretation A says X while Interpretation B says Y” answers the wrong question and caps your mark at the middle band.

Reasons why interpretations differ include: the time at which the historian wrote (a 1920s historian writing in the shadow of the anti-war poets will reach different conclusions from a 1990s revisionist with access to new archives); the historian’s purpose (academic history vs popular history vs political history); the evidence they prioritised (war poets vs soldiers’ diaries vs military statistics); and any political or ideological perspective that shapes their questions.

Question: Compare Interpretations A (traditional view that the First World War was necessary to resist German militarism) and B (Ferguson’s revisionist argument that Britain need not have entered) in terms of why they differ.

Weak: “Interpretation A says the war was necessary and B says it wasn’t. They differ because one agrees with the war and one doesn’t.”

Strong structure: “The interpretations differ partly because of when they were written: the traditional view was formed in a period when resisting German militarism seemed self-evidently justified; Ferguson wrote in the 1990s post-Cold War era when empire and military intervention were being reassessed across Western culture. They also differ in the questions asked: the traditional view asks ‘Was entering the war the right thing to do?’, while Ferguson asks the counterfactual ‘Was it necessary?’ — a different question that opens different evidence. Finally, they differ in the evidence used: Ferguson had access to post-war German archives showing the limits of German war aims; earlier historians did not.”

The 12-Mark and 16-Mark Essays

Both extended essays share the same requirement: a substantiated overall judgement. This means your conclusion must do more than summarise your paragraphs. It must directly answer the question with a precise claim: “The transformation of Britain was more significant in its political and welfare dimensions than in gender or imperial terms.”

Common mistakes in the 12-mark “Evaluate an Interpretation” question: writing only agreement, or only disagreement. The mark scheme explicitly requires you to “agree and disagree” with the interpretation using your own contextual knowledge. Examiners call a response that only agrees a “one-sided essay” — it cannot reach the top band regardless of how accurate the agreement is.

Key Fact

Top-band essays on transformation argue that change was significant but uneven — real in politics and welfare, partial in gender rights, and complicated in empire. A weak conclusion says “both sides have valid points.” A strong conclusion says which side is more convincing and why.

Exam Technique Checklist

Before you write your answer, check:

  • Source utility: Have I addressed content, provenance AND contextual knowledge together — not in three separate bullets?
  • Compare interpretations: Am I explaining why they differ (time, purpose, evidence, perspective) — not just what they say?
  • 12-mark evaluate: Have I agreed AND disagreed, both with specific evidence?
  • 16-mark essay: Have I reached a substantiated overall judgement that directly answers the question — not just summarised my paragraphs?
exam_tip_html: Timing matters. The source questions and short-answer questions come first — don’t spend so long on source utility (5 marks) that you rush the 12-mark or 16-mark essays where most marks are available. For the 12-mark and 16-mark questions, spend two minutes planning before writing. A clear plan with three analytical points and a direction for your conclusion produces a much sharper essay than writing without planning.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Source utility requires content, provenance and contextual knowledge together. Saying a source is biased does not make it useless — assess it for the specific enquiry asked.
  • The 10-mark ‘Compare Interpretations’ question is answered by explaining why interpretations differ (time written, purpose, evidence used) — not just describing what each says.
  • 12-mark and 16-mark essays must agree AND disagree (12-mark), or argue both sides (16-mark), and always reach a substantiated overall judgement — not just a summary.

practice_questions.text: A source describes women working in a munitions factory in 1916, written by the factory manager for a government report. How useful is this source for understanding the role of women on the Home Front during the First World War?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (4-5): Integrates content, provenance and contextual knowledge. Content: describes women's factory roles and conditions. Provenance: written by a manager for a government report — may understate dangers (TNT exposure, 'canary girls') to satisfy official oversight; written from a management perspective not workers'. Contextual knowledge: by 1918 ~800,000 women were in munitions; this source reflects the scale of women's industrial contribution that underpinned the case for the vote. Limitation: the management perspective means it may not capture women's actual experience of the work. Secure (2-3): addresses two elements. Developing (1): addresses one element only.

practice_questions.text: Compare what two sources about the concentration camps during the Boer War suggest about Britain's conduct of the war. (Assume Source A is an official government report minimising deaths; Source B is Emily Hobhouse's 1901 report.)
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per source comparison. Source A: official government minimisation — useful as evidence of the government's desire to manage public opinion; limited as evidence of actual conditions. Source B: Hobhouse's report — valuable as eyewitness evidence of conditions, with specific data on mortality; provenance: a campaigner with access and no financial interest in exaggerating — gives it credibility; contextual knowledge confirms the Fawcett Commission broadly endorsed her findings. The key comparison: both describe the same events but the difference in purpose (government defence vs humanitarian exposure) explains the divergence. Mastering: precise comparison addressing both provenance and content.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why historians might interpret the importance of the NUWSS differently from the importance of the WSPU in winning women the vote.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6): Historians writing in different eras ask different questions: earlier histories focused on the dramatic militant tactics of the WSPU (Pankhursts, Emily Davison) because they were more visible in the historical record; from the 1970s feminist historians recovering the NUWSS's records emphasised the 20-year constitutional campaign that created the legal and political groundwork; access to NUWSS organisational records (54,000 members, 400+ societies by 1913) changed the evidential basis. The interpretation also depends on which factors the historian weighs most heavily for 1918 — short-term militancy or long-term constitutional pressure. Secure (3-4): clear reason. Developing (1-2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: 'The propaganda techniques used by the government during the First World War successfully maintained public support until the armistice.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Agree and disagree, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: recruitment posters, censored press, Somme film (~20 million viewers within 6 weeks) maintained public engagement in critical early years; DORA suppressed open dissent; white feather campaigns enforced social conformity; propaganda gave people a narrative of heroism and necessity. Disagree: by 1917 casualty lists contradicted optimistic propaganda; Sassoon's 1917 protest was not suppressed but declared shell shock — showing limits of control; war poetry circulated despite censorship; food shortages and influenza in 1918 created real hardship propaganda could not address. Balanced: propaganda was essential in 1914-16 but was increasingly strained by 1917; public support held partly from genuine patriotism and investment in the lives already lost, not propaganda alone. Secure (7-9). Developing (4-6). Emerging (1-3): one-sided.

practice_questions.text: 'The Liberal reforms of 1906-1911 were the most important development in Britain in the period 1890-1918.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (13-16): Sustained argument, multiple themes, substantiated judgement. Agree: Liberal reforms established the principle of state welfare responsibility; helped hundreds of thousands immediately; created the administrative machinery of national insurance; directly prefigured the 1945 welfare state; driven by overwhelming evidence from Booth and Rowntree. Counter-arguments: Parliament Act 1911 had more immediate constitutional significance; women's suffrage represented a more fundamental change in who could participate in democracy; the First World War's impact (loss of 750,000, changed women's roles, imperial questions) was arguably more transformative in its scale. Judgement: the Liberal reforms were the most important domestic policy development but may be less 'transformative' overall than the constitutional changes or the war's social impact. Secure (9-12): argument covered, some judgement. Developing (5-8): partial. Emerging (1-4): simple listing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Suffragette campaign for the eventual achievement of women's suffrage in 1918.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): At the time: kept the issue in public debate through militant action; Emily Davison's death brought international attention; Cat and Mouse Act showed government's difficulty managing the campaign; however, the WSPU suspended its campaign in 1914 and did not directly cause the 1918 Act. Over time: Suffragette symbolism (Pankhursts, Davison) became central to how women's suffrage was remembered and celebrated; influenced later feminist movements globally; the WSPU's tactics became a model for civil disobedience movements in the twentieth century. Assessment: significant for publicity and maintaining urgency, but the wartime service and NUWSS constitutional groundwork were arguably more directly causal for 1918. Secure (5-6). Developing (3-4). Emerging (1-2).

knowledge_checks.q: For the 5-mark Source Utility question, which THREE elements must be integrated together?
For the 10-mark Compare Interpretations question, what is the key thing you must explain?
options: Which interpretation you personally agree with

knowledge_checks.q: For the 12-mark 'Evaluate an Interpretation' question, you must both _____ with the interpretation before reaching an overall judgement.
A _____ overall judgement in an extended essay means directly answering the question with a precise claim, not just summarising what you wrote.
Match each question type to its key requirement:
right: Agree AND disagree using own contextual knowledge, then judge
Explain WHY interpretations differ — not just HOW they differ
Integrate content, provenance and contextual knowledge together

flashcard_questions.a: How valuable a piece of evidence is for answering a specific historical question.

flashcard_questions.q: What three things must you weigh together for source utility?
Why does saying a source is 'biased' not make it useless?
flashcard_questions.a: Its bias can itself be valuable evidence — e.g. a propaganda poster is useful evidence of government propaganda methods.

flashcard_questions.q: For the 'Compare Interpretations' question, what is the banned approach?
flashcard_questions.a: Simply describing what each interpretation says — you must explain WHY they differ.

flashcard_questions.q: What four factors cause interpretations to differ?
flashcard_questions.a: Time written, purpose, evidence used, and the historian's own values or perspective.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a 'substantiated overall judgement' mean in an essay?
flashcard_questions.a: A conclusion that directly answers the question with a precise, evidence-supported claim — not a summary.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key mistake students make in the 12-mark 'Evaluate an Interpretation' question?
flashcard_questions.a: Writing only agreement or only disagreement — both are required for the top band.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between explaining HOW two interpretations differ and explaining WHY they differ?
flashcard_questions.a: HOW = what each says; WHY = the reasons (time, purpose, evidence, values) behind the different conclusions.

flashcard_questions.q: For the 16-mark period essay, what must the conclusion include beyond summarising the argument?
flashcard_questions.a: A direct answer to the question with a precise judgement about which factors were most significant.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'provenance' mean when analysing a historical source?
flashcard_questions.a: Who produced the source, when, why, and for what audience.

glossary_terms.definition: Assessment of how valuable a piece of evidence is for answering a specific historical question, weighed through content, provenance and contextual knowledge.
The factors that cause historians to reach different conclusions, including when they wrote, their purpose, the evidence they used, and their own values or perspective.
A final paragraph in an extended history essay that directly answers the question, weighs the arguments, and reaches a precise overall conclusion supported by evidence.
